title: John of the Cross, again
tomorrow: a monk said everyone wears a mask. so who's underneath?

segments.voice: Mark, again: straightway, still. A Gospel in a hurry, and a road still open. Today a slower teacher, one who learned his best lesson in the dark.
screen: `STRAIGHTWAY, STILL.` → `A TEACHER WHO LEARNED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Three in the morning is its own country. The phone is face-down, the ceiling feels too close, and every worry has a microphone. A friar in Spain knew that hour better than most. It's night in Toledo. He's locked in a cramped cell with little light, put there by men of his own religious order who opposed his reforms. And in the dark he's making up poems, holding every line in his memory. One night, tradition says, he knots strips of cloth into a rope, lowers himself from a window and slips away through the streets. So why would he later write about that kind of night as a gift?
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `A CELL IN TOLEDO.` → `A ROPE OF CLOTH, A WINDOW, THE STREET.`

segments.voice: He's John of the Cross, and the poem he carried out of that cell begins, in his Spanish, en una noche oscura: on a dark night. A soul slips out of a quiet house, unseen, with no light to guide it except the one burning in its own heart. He later wrote whole books unpacking that poem, and the dark night became his name for something that happens in prayer. The sweetness fades. The old feeling of closeness goes flat. Prayer that used to glow feels like talking to a wall. John's surprise is that this isn't proof God has gone. His books say the night loosens our grip on the good feelings, so love can grow for God himself, not just for the glow. Something to tell a friend tonight: people now say dark night of the soul about any rough season. John meant something narrower and stranger, a darkness that teaches. Not every hard night is that one. Grief and depression need people and real help, and if a night ever feels dangerous, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help. But looking back down the mountain, John's claim is simple. He walked out of that cell carrying poems. The night taught.
screen: `EN UNA NOCHE OSCURA.` · `WHEN PRAYER GOES FLAT.` · `NOT PROOF THAT GOD HAS GONE.` · `A DARKNESS THAT TEACHES.` · then, large: `THE NIGHT TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and anything to write on. Remember one night, or one hard stretch, that taught you something you still carry, and write down only what it taught, in a few words. Rest your hand on the page for the sit; anyone who prays can offer it to God along with the night it came from.
John of the Cross. A Spanish friar and poet who named the dark night, a darkness in prayer that teaches.
Your line: the night taught. He walked out of that cell with a poem. See you tomorrow.

fork.setup: a friend says prayer has felt flat for months and she's sure it means she's doing it wrong. what would John of the Cross say first?

she should stop praying until the feeling comes back.

fork.reveal: John called that dryness part of the dark night: it loosens our grip on the good feelings so love can grow for God himself.

chat.says: coach from my dream school went silent. three weeks. is that a sign i should just quit?
options: Not a sign by itself. Hard stretches can teach you things; don't decide it all at 3am.
Yes. A dark night means God left the room, so pick a brand new dream now.
John of the Cross says suffering is good, so just enjoy the silence and wait.
chat.meaning: For John, the dark isn't proof that God has gone; it can teach what the light can't. The night taught.
